- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.3) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% relative to prior high.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model often overshoots in next 5–7 days — cap forecast at +3–5% above prior peak.
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (0.0–0.3) and price is trending upward, model underestimates continuation — add 2–4% to forecast for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is consistently negative over 5+ days, model tends to underestimate true decline — adjust downward by 3–7% for next 7–10 days.
- Model often overestimates short-term (1–3 day) reversals — if sentiment shifts from negative to positive, delay forecast reversal by 1–2 days and reduce magnitude.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to overestimate mean reversion — if recent 18-day average is rising, forecast should be slightly below that average to avoid overcorrection.
- If sentiment is positive and price is near 30-day high, model often overestimates peak — reduce forecast by 3–6% for next 5–7 days to avoid “peak inflation” bias.
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–0.2–0.4), model tends to overfit short-term noise — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ values before applying sentiment-weighted adjustment.
